This is one of the most popular and widely sold permanent box colors in the country, sitting on almost every drugstore shelf. Like most permanent dyes, it colors hair through oxidation, where a colorless chemical called paraffenolamine, better known as PPD, mixes with peroxide and locks pigment deep inside every strand. PPD comes from colar, and it is the exact ingredient family that scientists keep putting under the microscope. One large review published in 2022 looked at long-term hair dye users [music] and found roughly a 10% higher overall cancer risk when compared to people who never colored their hair. The real concern is not a single box on a single day. It is the slow buildup from coloring [music] again and again every four to 6 weeks across many years. Because color silk is so common and so easy to grab off the shelf, many people use it for decades without ever [music] reading the back of the pack. That habit repeated hundreds of times is exactly the kind of long-term exposure those studies were measuring. The challenge is built right into that strength because the darkest browns and blacks need the highest amounts of the coloring chemicals to work. As health groups explain, deeper permanent shades carry more PPD and related aromatic amines than lighter ones. So, the very results people love come with the heaviest chemical dose. segments.text: Researchers point out that the body clears most PPD through urine within about 24 hours, which sounds reassuring until you remember most users repeat the process every [music] month for years.

segments.text: None of this means a single use is a verdict on anyone, but it does mean the people most loyal to dark permanent shades may be carrying more exposure over time than they realize.
